children: What Happened?

A number of stocks fell in the afternoon session after hotter-than-expected economic data showed U.S. inflation climbing to 3.7% year over year in September, stoking investor concerns over stubborn price pressures and rising bond yields. September CPI rose 3.7% from a year earlier, above the 3.6% economist consensus, after a 0.6% monthly gain that was driven in large part by higher gasoline prices alongside firmer costs for apparel and airfares. That mix matters for restaurant operators on both sides of the P&L: energy and transport inflation lift input and delivery costs, while higher living costs—especially at the pump—can push households to cut back on discretionary dining-out spend. Broader indices moved lower as investors priced a greater chance that borrowing costs stay elevated, and when yields rise with inflation, equity valuations typically compress because future earnings are discounted at higher rates. Restaurant stocks, which are closely tied to consumer traffic and menu-price elasticity, were among the names that sold off as that macro backdrop weighed on the group.
The stock market overreacts to news, and big price drops can present good opportunities to buy high-quality stocks.

Zooming In On Shake Shack (SHAK)

Shake Shack’s shares are very volatile and have had 22 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today’s move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.

The previous big move we wrote about was 29 days ago when the stock dropped 4% on the news that Restaurant Stocks Drop Following Nationwide Decline in Dining Foot Traffic. Foot traffic across U.S. dining chains fell 2.4% year-over-year in August amid weakening consumer sentiment and elevated living costs, according to Placer.ai’s August 2026 Retail and Dining Index.According to Placer.ai, dining locations nationwide saw reduced visitor volume as average gasoline prices stayed above $4 per gallon throughout August and menu-price inflation continued to weigh on discretionary spending. Food-away-from-home prices rose 3.4% year-over-year, outpacing a 2.2% increase for groceries and reinforcing the shift toward eating at home. Sustained weaker traffic pressures restaurant operators by reducing sales volumes and limiting their ability to absorb elevated labor and operating costs without further menu price hikes. With consumer budgets still constrained by macroeconomic pressures, investors are growing more cautious about margin compression and slower revenue growth across the dining and hospitality sector.

Shake Shack is down 17.5% since the beginning of the year, and at $68.85 per share, it is trading 34.2% below its 52-week high of $104.69 from April 2026. Investors who bought $1,000 worth of Shake Shack’s shares 5 years ago would now be looking at only $896.83.
